> Academia has been treating it has if it were true for the last half a century because everyone was "pretty sure" that it was,

Which conjecture do you mean, and what do you mean by “academia treated it as true”? If a paper proves “assuming X, we can guarantee Y,” the assumption still matters. A proof of X removes that condition from every valid result that depended on it, while leaving any other assumptions in place. That’s a concrete change even if every author involved already expected X to be true.
Failure to find a counterexample can justify confidence. It doesn’t tell us what happens in every untested case. And Gödel’s theorem says that certain formal systems contain some statements they can neither prove nor disprove. To claim that this particular conjecture is one of them, you’d need a separate argument identifying the system and establishing that result.
I agree that a counterexample could have been more surprising. It would show exactly where a widely held expectation breaks down. A proof would establish when people can safely rely on it. Which outcome is more valuable depends on what others could do with each one. Even if a counterexample would have been worth more, that hardly makes a proof worthless.

>Even if Anthropic had produced a proof (they haven't),
Levent Alpöge released a formal proof of the Riemann hypothesis developed with Claude. On November 21st, the Lean and Mathlib communities published their verification. They checked two things that matter: Does the code prove the actual Riemann hypothesis? And is the proof valid? Two independent tools confirmed that the theorem matched the established statement of the hypothesis, and several independently implemented proof checkers validated the proof.

But I have a feeling you're just going to move goalposts and deny it...

And yet, there is no shortage of people providing bogus claims that attempt to convince others that they do, in fact, understand or comprehend. This is because they, and even you, intuitively understand that an answer alone is not nearly as valuable as the process to obtain an answer. This is more than mere semantics, all answers are necessarily based on incomplete, imperfect, or just plain wrong information. A good answer, one that shows its work, can incorporate small changes to its inputs with small amounts of work. LLMs cannot do this, they must start over from the very beginning, because they cannot "show their work", nor can they understand a process and follow or tweak it as they go, they can only start over from the very beginning, they can just do so at enormous scale, which is the basis of agentic loops. LLMs cannot modify or change how they work on the fly. A human mind can build a model of what it knows, and, in LLM terminology, dynamically compress and decompress its "context" to suite what is important at a given time. An LLM must re-process its entire context every time, or rely on its human operator to lossfully and inelegantly compress previous context. An LLM is incapable of reflecting on its own history and revising its context. These are all things that a human mind can do without even consciously thinking about it, but that LLMs are definitionally incapable of, and they have direct consequences on not just their output, but their ability to sustain their output into the future. Perhaps there is a future, as of yet undiscovered model of computation that can more accurately do these things that could conceivable be called "AI", but LLMs are not it, and will never be it.

I think it depends a whole lot on how you define free market capitalism, and it’s a little more slippery than people give it credit for. For example, the roots of free market capitalism can be found in decidedly global trade systems (slave trade to Saint Domingue/Barbados/ capital gained from imperial projects infused money into a lot of the proto industrial movement, and capitalism as we understand it wouldn’t exist without global connection. I’d argue that it has NOT existed without global trade systems underpinning it. It’s important I think to agree on what “capitalism” is first and foremost because a lot of people mistakenly believe that it is simply a society with a free market. For me and for a lot of historians/economists, a capitalist society (as opposed to a feudalist/socialist/communist/mercantilist one) is one in which the society is organized around accruing capital in order to reinvest and consequently secure even more capital. Reinvestment in the pursuit of capital is a constitutive element. One can see how you could have a small town with a lively market center that is not necessarily capitalist in that the pursuit of capital is not the organizing principle of the society. Romans were not capitalists. Egyptians were not capitalists. Both had thriving trade.

So far as capitalist is understood in this way, it’s hard for me to imagine how it persists without the exploitation of labor at the periphery of capitalism’s core. Historically, it’s nearly always happened this way (and I use the word “nearly” because there are perhaps some exceptions to the rule that maybe I don’t know about, but I can’t think of them).

Experiences of pain in this category disrupt the ability of individuals to function optimally. Different from Annoying pain, the ability to draw attention away from the sensation of pain is reduced: awareness of pain is likely to be present most of the time, interspersed by brief periods during which pain can be ignored depending on the level of distraction provided by other activities. Individuals can still conduct routine activities that are important in the short-term (e.g. eating, foraging) and perform cognitively demanding tasks, but an impairment in their ability or motivation to do so is likely to be observed. Although animals may still engage in behaviors they are strongly motivated to perform (i.e., exploratory, comfort, sexual, and maintenance behaviors), their frequency or duration is likely to be reduced. Engagement in positive activities with no immediate benefits (e.g., play in piglets, dustbathing in chickens) is not expected. Reduced alertness and inattention to ongoing stimuli may be present. The effect of (effective) drugs (e.g., analgesics if the pain is physical, psychotropic drugs in the case of psychological pain) in the alleviation of symptoms is expected.

There’s two other categories (disabling and excruciating) but I don’t think most wagies experience these on the job or off the job caused by the job

DISABLING PAIN

Pain at this level takes priority over most bids for behavioral execution and prevents all forms of enjoyment or positive welfare. Pain is continuously distressing. Individuals affected by harms in this category often change their activity levels drastically (the degree of disruption in the ability of an organism to function optimally should not be confused with the overt expression of pain behaviors, which is less likely in prey species). Inattention and unresponsiveness to ongoing stimuli and surroundings are likely to be observed. Relief often requires higher drug dosages or more powerful drugs. The term Disabling refers to the disability caused by ‘pain’, not to any structural disability.
